{{Short description|Theorem in mathematical measure theory}}
In [[mathematics]], more precisely in [[measure theory]], the '''Lebesgue decomposition theorem'''{{sfn|Hewitt|Stromberg|1965|loc=Chapter&nbsp;V, §&nbsp;19, (19.42) Lebesgue Decomposition Theorem}} provides a way to decompose a measure into two distinct parts based on their relationship with another measure. 

==Formal Statement==
The theorem states that if <math>(\Omega,\Sigma)</math> is a [[measurable space]] and <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu</math> 
are [[sigma-finite measure|σ-finite]] [[signed measure]]s on <math>\Sigma</math>, then there exist two uniquely determined σ-finite signed measures <math>\nu_0</math> and <math>\nu_1</math> such that:{{sfn|Halmos|1974|loc=Section 32, Theorem C}}{{sfn|Swartz|1994|p=141}}

* <math>\nu=\nu_0+\nu_1\, </math>
* <math>\nu_0\ll\mu</math> (that is, <math>\nu_0</math> is [[Absolute continuity (measure theory)|absolutely continuous]] with respect to <math>\mu</math>)
* <math>\nu_1\perp\mu</math> (that is, <math>\nu_1</math> and <math>\mu</math> are [[Singular measure|singular]]).

===Refinement===
Lebesgue's decomposition theorem can be refined in a number of ways. First, as the '''Lebesgue–Radon–Nikodym theorem'''. That is, let  
<math>(\Omega,\Sigma)</math> be a measure space, <math>\mu</math> a [[sigma-finite measure|σ-finite]] [[positive measure]] on <math>\Sigma</math> and <math>\lambda</math> a [[complex measure]] on <math>\Sigma</math>.{{sfn|Rudin|1974|loc=Section 6.9, The Theorem of Lebesgue–Radon–Nikodym}}
* There is a unique pair of complex measures on <math>\Sigma</math> such that <math display="block">\lambda = \lambda_a + \lambda_s, \quad \lambda_a \ll \mu, \quad \lambda_s \perp \mu.</math> If <math>\lambda</math> is positive and finite, then so are <math>\lambda_a</math> and <math>\lambda_s</math>.
* There is a unique <math>h \in L^1(\mu)</math> such that <math display="block">\lambda_a (E) = \int_E h d\mu, \quad E \in \Sigma.</math>
The first assertion follows from the Lebesgue decomposition, the second is known as the [[Radon–Nikodym theorem]]. That is, the function <math>h</math> is a Radon–Nikodym derivative that can be expressed as
<math display="block">h = \frac{d\lambda_a}{d\mu}.</math>

An alternative refinement is that of the decomposition of a regular [[Borel measure]]{{sfn|Hewitt|Stromberg|1965|loc=Chapter V, § 19, (19.61) Theorem}}{{sfn|Reed|Simon|1981|pp=22-25}}{{sfn|Simon|2005|p=43}}
<math display="block">\nu = \nu_{ac} + \nu_{sc} + \nu_{pp},</math>
where
* <math>\nu_{ac} \ll \mu</math> is the '''absolutely continuous''' part
* <math>\nu_{sc} \perp \mu</math> is the '''singular continuous''' part
* <math>\nu_{pp}</math> is the '''pure point''' part (a [[discrete measure]]).

The absolutely continuous measures are classified by the [[Radon–Nikodym theorem]], and discrete measures are easily understood. Hence (singular continuous measures aside), Lebesgue decomposition gives a very explicit description of measures.  The [[Cantor measure]] (the [[probability measure]] on the [[real line]] whose [[cumulative distribution function]] is the [[Cantor function]]) is an example of a singular continuous measure.

==Related concepts==

===Lévy–Itō decomposition===
{{Main|Lévy–Itō decomposition}}
The analogous{{citation needed|date=January 2017}} decomposition for a [[stochastic processes]] is the [[Lévy–Itō decomposition]]: given a [[Lévy process]] ''X,'' it can be decomposed as a sum of three independent [[Lévy process]]es <math>X=X^{(1)}+X^{(2)}+X^{(3)}</math> where:
* <math>X^{(1)}</math> is a [[Brownian motion]] with drift, corresponding to the absolutely continuous part;
* <math>X^{(2)}</math> is a [[compound Poisson process]], corresponding to the pure point part;
* <math>X^{(3)}</math> is a [[square integrable]] pure jump [[Martingale (probability theory)|martingale]] that almost surely has a countable number of jumps on a finite interval, corresponding to the singular continuous part.
